claims.text: The Space Station flies about 400 kilometres up.
At that height, Earth's gravity is still about 90 percent as strong as on the ground.
≈ 90 % of ground-level gravity, at the Space Station
But it's also racing sideways, at about 28,000 kilometres an hour.

At the International Space Station's altitude (200–250 miles, about 320–400 km), Earth's gravity is still about 90% as strong as on the ground. Astronauts float because they're in free fall: the station, the crew and everything aboard are constantly falling toward Earth while racing sideways at 17,500 mph (about 28,000 km/h), so they keep falling around it instead.

review.notes: NASA (What Is Microgravity, grades 5-8): ISS at 200–250 miles (320–400 km; 'about 400 km' is the upper end and matches typical ISS altitude); gravity about 90% of the surface value; astronauts float because they are in free fall, falling toward but around Earth; 17,500 mph = 28,164 km/h ('about 28,000'). NASA Glenn: 'many people mistakenly think gravity does not exist in space'. The title states the truth, so the hook does not reinforce the myth. Photos are captioned by NASA (ISS 2018, Meir with a water sphere 2020).
